question.text: Which of the following is an ASSUMPTION of the Black-Scholes option pricing model?

answer.text: Volatility of the underlying remains constant over the option's life
Markets are inefficient and arbitrage opportunities persist
Options can be exercised at any time before expiry (American style)
Transaction costs and taxes significantly affect option prices

explanation.text: The Logic: The classical Black-Scholes-Merton option-pricing model is derived under a set of simplifying assumptions, most importantly: the underlying follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility, European-style exercise (no early exercise), a constant risk-free rate, no transaction costs or taxes, frictionless and arbitrage-free markets, and (in the basic version) no dividends. Constant volatility is the standard textbook assumption — real markets show a volatility smile / term structure precisely because this assumption is violated. The Trap: "Markets are inefficient and arbitrage opportunities persist" reverses the assumption — the model assumes no-arbitrage efficient markets. "Options can be exercised at any time" describes American exercise, which Black-Scholes does NOT assume. "Transaction costs and taxes significantly affect option prices" contradicts the frictionless-market assumption. Note: The cited NISM Series VIII Equity Derivatives workbook lists the inputs to Black-Scholes (stock price, strike, volatility, time, risk-free rate; dividends ignored), but the pages checked do not explicitly list "constant volatility" as a model assumption. The assumption set above is general option-pricing theory.
